self-play.d: Training (or using) a model by having it interact with copies of itself, with a previous version or with itself in another role. The adversary improves alongside it, which creates an automatic curriculum; in LLMs, someone still has to decide who referees.

supervisao-escalavel.d: The problem of supervising a model more capable than the supervisor (human or model), when the judge cannot verify the answer alone. Debate and prover-verifier games are proposals to solve it.

debate-ia.d: Proposal by Irving, Christiano and Amodei (2018): two agents take turns making short statements about a question and a judge picks the winner, in a zero-sum game. Hypothesis: refuting a lie is easier than sustaining it, so optimal play is honest.

argumentos-ofuscados.d: A theoretical failure of debate: the dishonest debater decomposes a claim so that not even the honest one can locate, in reasonable time, the wrong part. Prover-estimator debate (2025) is a proposal to get around it.

consultoria.d: Baseline of the debate studies: a single expert defends one answer, which is right only half the time, and the judge decides whether to believe it. In the study by Michael et al., the judge was right 74% of the time here versus 84% in debate.

assimetria-de-informacao.d: A situation in which the debater has access to something the judge does not (the text, the code, the output of a tool). Kenton et al. (2024) only saw debate beat direct questioning in these cases.

self-consistency.d: Sampling several independent answers from the same model (with temperature > 0) and keeping the one with the most votes. It is the fair baseline for multi-agent debate: compare the two with the same number of generated tokens.

spin.d: Method by Chen et al. (2024): iteration \(t+1\) learns to distinguish human SFT responses from responses generated by iteration \(t\). With a logistic loss, it is a DPO with chosen = human, rejected = its own generation and reference = previous iteration; the fixed point is \(p_\theta = p_{\text{data}}\).

ponto-fixo.d: A state in which one iteration of the loop no longer changes the model. In SPIN, it happens when the model's responses have the same distribution as the human ones and the discriminator can no longer tell them apart.

self-rewarding.d: Loop by Yuan et al. (2024): the model generates prompts and candidates, judges them with a 5-point rubric and trains with DPO on the (highest score, lowest score) pairs. On Llama 2 70B, AlpacaEval 2.0 went from 9.94% to 20.44%.

llm-as-judge.d: Using an LLM, instructed with a rubric or a reference, to evaluate or compare responses in place of a human. It has known biases: position, verbosity, self-preference and limited reasoning.

rubrica-aditiva.d: A scoring scheme in which each criterion met adds one point. In Self-Rewarding there are 5 criteria (relevance, coverage, usefulness, clarity and expertise), for a score from 0 to 5.

meta-rewarding.d: Extension of Self-Rewarding (Wu et al., 2024) in which the model also judges its own judgments, so that its judging ability does not saturate. Llama-3-8B-Instruct: AlpacaEval 2 from 22.9% to 39.4%.

autopreferencia.d: Bias of an LLM judge that gives its own outputs higher scores than humans would. It grows with the model's ability to recognize itself (Panickssery, Bowman and Feng, 2024). The mitigation is to use a judge from another family or a panel.

preferencia-intransitiva.d: Preferences that form a cycle (A beats B, B beats C, C beats A), as in Condorcet's paradox. No scalar score, and therefore no Bradley–Terry model, can represent them.

equilibrio-de-nash.d: A pair of strategies in which no player gains by changing alone. In SPPO's preference game, it is the policy that wins at least half of the matchups against any other policy.

modelo-de-preferencia-pareado.d: A model that takes a prompt and two responses and returns \(\mathbb P(y \succ y')\) directly, without going through a scalar score. SPPO uses PairRM, with 0.4B parameters. Unlike the scalar PM of RL-CAI (chapter 60).

pesos-multiplicativos.d: An update in which each option is multiplied by \(e^{\eta\cdot\text{gain}}\) and the total is renormalized. In zero-sum games, the average of the iterates converges to the equilibrium, while the last iterate can circle around and, with a constant step, drift away from it. It is the ideal update that SPPO approximates by regression.

sppo.d: Method by Wu et al. (2024) that treats alignment as a constant-sum game and seeks the Nash equilibrium: it regresses each response's log-ratio toward \(\eta(\mathbb P(y\succ\pi_t) - \tfrac12)\). In TRL: loss_type=["sppo_hard"], beta=0.001.

absolute-zero.d: Method by Zhao et al. (2025) in which a single model proposes and solves code tasks (deduction, abduction and induction over program–input–output triples), verified by a Python executor, with no curated data at all.

recompensa-de-aprendibilidade.d: The proposer's reward in Absolute Zero: \(1 - \bar r_{\text{solve}}\) if the solver succeeds sometimes, and 0 if it never or always succeeds. It pushes the tasks to the edge of the current skill.

trr-plus-plus.d: Absolute Zero's advantage estimator, with 6 separate baselines (3 task types × 2 roles): \(A = (r - \mu_{\text{task,role}})/\sigma_{\text{task,role}}\).

ilusao-de-diversidade.d: R-Diverse's (2026) diagnosis of task self-play: diversity measured only within the batch hides cycles across iterations, and surface variety hides the repetition of the same skills.

jogo-prover-verifier.d: A game between a powerful prover and a limited verifier, designed so that the equilibrium forces checkable answers. Kirchner et al. (2024) train helpful provers, sneaky provers and small verifiers in rounds, and the legibility transfers to humans.

lei-de-goodhart.d: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” In post-training: optimizing a judge's or an RM's score makes the score go up while real quality peaks and then falls.
